articles.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
articles.author: Naisha Roy
paras: The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.

About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.
Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.

The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way.
“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica.

A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.

ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector, a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.

Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer. All but one passed every test.

The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”
In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns.

In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.”

Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense.

“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”

ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness.
“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.”

articles.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
articles.author: Andy Kroll
paras: A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.

In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”

Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.

In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.

“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”

Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.
“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.

Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.

Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.

Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”
Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”
“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote.
Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.
“Over my dead body,” he wrote.

articles.title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
articles.author: Rob Davis
paras: When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning.

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.
Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.

JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.

A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.
Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.

JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.
Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”

“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”

Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.

Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.
“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”

De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.
“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.
Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.
Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)

Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.

ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.

Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.

ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.

The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government.

Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.

Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing subsidies. Since 2024, Oregon has given the money on a first-come, first-served basis. When funding runs out, Bell’s agency places applications on a waitlist in the order received.

Bell spoke with Washington County officials about Aloha 209th during a 45-minute Zoom meeting in August, records show. Internal notes summarizing the conversation say that the county would send an updated report to the state agency to “inform movement of 209.” The summary said the groups involved would have a follow-up conversation about the project.

Bell went on to discuss the project with regional government officials in early September. About two weeks before the meeting, she emailed her deputy with two possible ways to get the project funded: a legislative “carve-out” or Metro consolidating its subsidies so it could fully pay for the project. “I want to do everything we can to help the metro projects be successful and the resources, like ours, are nearly depleted,” Bell wrote. She acknowledged that Metro might not find the solution appealing.
Bell told ProPublica that she met with Metro and Washington County at the other agencies’ request. She said her agency “does not have and is not pursuing a ‘legislative carve out’ for any project.”

“My approach is to listen to partners’ concerns and explain our funding process,” she said in an email. “I have no role in deciding whether projects should receive funding as part of this process, and I do not advocate for individual projects. Characterizing these routine discussions and legitimate concerns as something improper fundamentally misrepresents their purpose and context.”

A spokesperson for Washington County’s housing authority told ProPublica that Bell did not make any commitment to alter the prioritization of Aloha 209th. Another Washington County spokesperson said the August meeting with Bell was mainly focused on the housing authority’s desire for “clearer criteria” for how projects on the state’s waitlist get funded.
A Metro spokesperson said the regional agency requested the September meeting with a goal “for the two agencies to strengthen our working relationship and coordination.”

“Metro does not, and did not, advocate for any specific project,” the spokesperson said. “We clearly indicated this at the meeting and in writing ahead of the meeting.” The agency has advocated for a group of remaining projects, including Aloha 209th, to get money so Metro can fulfill commitments made as part of its affordable housing bond, the spokesperson said.

Oregon’s Government Ethics Commission has until early December to complete its preliminary review of the complaint over Bell’s financial disclosure, which will help the agency decide whether to open a full investigation.
Bell said she will “continue to remain responsive to the Ethics Commission” as it completes its examination.

Kotek’s office, provided with a list of ProPublica’s latest findings, said in a statement that the governor “holds all agency leadership to consistent and high ethical standards” and that her office “is closely following” the ethics panel’s review.
The post Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset
articles.author: Agnel Philip
paras: For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration.

For example, last year my colleagues uncovered a dramatic rise in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The number of blood transfusions during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well.

Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level. We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality.
The increase was particularly stark in states that had banned abortion.

This was a significant and serious finding. And as far as we could tell, the fact that the number of women who died from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled after abortion bans came into effect hadn’t been reported before.

A death from an ectopic pregnancy should be a “never event,” according to Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia. And yet, as we later confirmed, more than a dozen leaders in the field of maternal health were unaware of the spike. Neither state governments nor the federal government, whose own dataset we were using, had publicly identified this trend.
How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us?

The answer, as it turns out, is multifold and begins with the nature of the condition itself. Ectopic pregnancies occur when an embryo fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The pregnancy grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding.
It is a rare condition, estimated to impact up to 2% of pregnancies, but it is incredibly dangerous.
“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023.

“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in an ongoing lawsuit challenging an abortion ban, after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.”

Even before ectopic pregnancy deaths began rising, the condition was noted as the leading cause of death in the first trimester of pregnancy. Yet it has received little research attention. For example, the CDC doesn’t track how many ectopic pregnancies occur a year and doesn’t require healthcare providers to report them. The most recent nationwide study we could find examined data only through 2013.

The U.S. doesn’t conduct national maternal mortality reviews in the same way as countries like the United Kingdom, which responded to a similar spike in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic by instituting changes to emergency services and promoting awareness of ectopic pregnancy symptoms. Instead, in our country, much of the work of investigating pregnancy-related deaths is left to state committees.

This creates a large potential knowledge gap. In individual states, the number of ectopic deaths is small and subject to a lot of variation, making it harder to spot a trend. After our story was published, we reached out to maternal mortality review committees in states with abortions bans; many of them responded that they didn’t identify an increase in ectopic deaths and that, despite the findings of our reporting, they had no plans to examine this issue further.
We realized the fact that nearly double the number of women are dying from ectopic pregnancies is visible at only the national level.

It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. We reached out to the CDC to ask what the agency has done to investigate or address this trend. It has epidemiologists who review death and birth records and has in the past done its own investigations and analyses. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t provide a direct answer to that question but said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research.

Maternal experts agree that the government’s capacity to respond to this trend has been significantly reduced as a result of the staffing cuts initiated by the Trump administration since the beginning of last year. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year.
This lack of awareness surrounding ectopic pregnancy deaths is imperiling women’s lives.

We asked several experts why death rates were going up, but there was no consensus. And while our analysis can’t establish whether there is a causal link between abortion bans and the worse outcomes in the states that have them, there is no evidence that officials are stepping up to examine this question or offer solutions. Even professional organizations, such as the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, have yet to provide specific guidance to doctors about how to adequately treat women with suspected ectopic pregnancies in states with abortion bans.

But experts say the trend we uncovered is unacceptable and requires a response. As Courtney Schreiber, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology, told us, our work “raises concern that young women are dying from a preventable cause at an increasing rate. That is not what we should be seeing in the United States of America.”

We hope you’ll read our recent investigation, which includes more details on potential explanations for this trend and stories from women in states with abortion bans who faced delays in care. We plan to continue reporting on maternal health and the impact of abortion bans for the foreseeable future.
The post An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
articles.author: Robert Faturechi
paras: In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.
The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.
A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.

We’re still reporting. If you know anything about Trump Jr. or his businesses, please get in touch with our reporting team.
Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses.
The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.

According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.

The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.

The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.
Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.

The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it.

Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.

In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”

Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said.
Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.

In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.

1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.

This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.

1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.

It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part of. It’s also not clear if the White House played any role in Hadrian’s being considered, though defense documents about the deal mention the “White House and DoW leadership’s expressed need for advanced manufacturing” — which Hadrian specializes in.

In response to questions to the White House, an administration official said Hadrian reached out to the Pentagon proposing a loan and that “It is at an extremely early stage.” (The documents ProPublica reviewed show specific terms being considered by the Pentagon for the loan and discussions of its merits and risks.)

At the March ribbon cutting for the first of three factories to be built for submarine parts and systems for the Navy, Hadrian’s Australian-born founder, Chris Power, promised a radical change to defense manufacturing. “The number-one problem that the Navy’s identified is we can’t find enough skilled workers, so we have to automate our way out of this problem,” he told reporters. The factory will be run on its artificial intelligence software, called Opus, which Power said would make his production line more efficient and nimble.

The Navy “can’t hire enough people and the primes can’t hire enough people because there aren’t enough trained people to do it,” he said, referring to major defense contractors. “We need to automate and have people running multiple robots in a new way of doing things versus replacing jobs.”

Venture capital firms are betting heavily that the marriage of AI and robotics will lead to major upheaval in manufacturing sectors, investing $33 billion — more than all of last year — in just the first half of 2026, according to data from PitchBook.

When it comes to defense contracting, analysts have said that they expect only a handful of companies will succeed, with a wave of consolidations to follow. A mega Defense Department contract for Hadrian could position it as just such a winner — even as the company has shared few details publicly about what its AI-powered factories have so far been able to produce. In testimony before Congress last year, Power said only that the company had successfully fabricated parts for “missile systems, fighter jets, spacecraft and naval vessels.”Power started the company in 2020, saying he moved to the U.S. with just $6,000 and began cold-calling manufacturers looking to develop an idea to understand their operations and probe for bottlenecks. Much of the aerospace and defense industries, he found, relied on small shops with experts who were close to retirement. The solution, he decided, was automation.

Hadrian executives told Forbes in 2024 that the company spent its first two years trying to replicate components for two companies using its automation software in a small demonstration factory in California. It never named the companies or said which components it was able to replicate. It hired employees away from Elon Musk companies SpaceX and Tesla. It also hired employees from defense contractors Anduril, Raytheon and Palantir. Hadrian has also drawn investments from high-profile Silicon Valley funds, including Andreessen Horowitz and Altimeter Capital. The company has not released a recent employee count, but outside estimates put it at a few hundred.

This year, Hadrian has announced openings of new plants faster than outside analysts have been able to assess how well its operations are working. Mesa, Arizona, officials celebrated opening the company’s third factory in January. The ribbon cutting for its fourth, in Alabama for the Navy, took place in March, with Hadrian saying full production would begin in a couple of years.

A multibillion-dollar investment in Hadrian could push the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital far beyond the purpose for which it was approved and funded by Congress, some former defense officials said.

The office was created during the Biden administration to fill holes in the country’s industrial base so that the U.S. can stop relying on China, its top rival, to equip its own military. Under Trump, the lending unit has greatly expanded and focused on issuing loans to private companies to develop production of rare earth minerals and other technologies that have both commercial and military applications. That need has been elevated as the president’s tariff wars have heightened concerns that China could cut off the flow of critical minerals needed to produce high-tech weapons. The firms receiving loans generally make their money by supplying both defense contractors and other private-sector businesses.

But the idea of loaning money to Hadrian in hopes that it grows to become a major source of military munitions has sparked concerns within the Pentagon that the company would become reliant largely on the federal government.

When Congress created the Office of Strategic Capital, it included language prohibiting the OSC from making loans for projects with only military applications. A Pentagon document describing the proposed Hadrian loan indicates that the firm’s new factories would expand the U.S. capability to manufacture munitions and precision components for military use. The document states that Hadrian factories could “pivot rapidly to commercial applications.”

The former defense officials said the U.S. government might face allegations that it would be giving a distinct advantage to Hadrian over potential competitors. Other businesses could challenge whether the company is winning bids or subcontracting work on its merits or so that taxpayers do not lose on their capital investment.

David Lorch, a political appointee who heads up OSC, would have to sign off on the loan. Lorch previously worked at Cerberus, the private equity firm founded by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg. It’s unclear if Feinberg or others in the Trump administration would also have to approve the deal because of its size.

A former defense official familiar with the OSC said a Hadrian loan of that magnitude could put the lending unit’s credibility in jeopardy with the incoming Congress, which would likely have to approve additional funds to allow it to continue issuing new loans.

“OSC is clearly a powerful tool to advance national security. But its ability to invest and access to long-term funding are tenuous,” the official said. “Some senior leaders seemingly want to use it as a pot of money for deals that exceed its mandate.”

In the past, Trump Jr. and his firm have said he does not discuss the companies he invests in with federal officials. In his public comments, he has shown a personal interest in defense tech and has criticized cronyism in defense spending.
The Office of Strategic Capital was also behind the decision to give hundreds of millions of dollars in loans to Vulcan Elements just months after Trump Jr.’s venture firm invested in the company.

Of the dozens of companies the Pentagon was considering funding at the time, Vulcan’s was the only deal brought forward by a top aide to the president, ProPublica previously reported. After defense officials got the White House request, they asked Pentagon staff to move at an unusually rapid pace, and staff worked late nights and with little sleep to get the loan through in a matter of weeks.
The Pentagon denied any preferential treatment, and Trump Jr. said he played no role in the deal.

articles.title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
articles.author: Katie Worth
paras: A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.
Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.

The role of carbon capture was just one cause of discord in Turkey at the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, known as the Conference of the Parties. But it reflects a culmination of decades of effort by fossil fuel companies, and the nations most dependent on them, to slow a transition away from oil, coal and gas in part by pressing for methods like carbon capture, which theoretically allow for the use of their products and cleaning up carbon pollution at the same time.

Over the course of two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, drafts of the summit’s main political accord were stripped of language encouraging such a transition even as specific targets were added to expand carbon capture and storage, or CCS.

One draft released Nov. 16 included language encouraging a transition from fossil fuels alongside a recommendation to scale up carbon capture — where greenhouse gases are caught from industry, or filtered from the air, and injected underground — so that it removes at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide a year by 2035.

Currently, however, the carbon capture industry buries only a sliver of that amount and has struggled for three decades to meet even the lowest-end projections, leading many climate experts to conclude that it will never be a practical solution to climate change.

“The effort by bad faith petrostate actors to block any agreement at #COP31 on fossil fuel phaseout in favor of (hypothetical future) carbon capture is the best evidence yet that moral hazard FUNDAMENTALLY compromises carbon capture as a climate solution,” wrote Michael Mann, a prominent climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, in a Bluesky post Sunday.

As it stands, most CCS is used to squeeze additional oil from aging fields, so critics say setting global goals for it would lead to further subsidy of oil production, rather than limit or reduce the amount of CO2 that reaches the air.

Behind the scenes in Antalya, some 700 carbon capture lobbyists were registered as attending, up from 531 at last year’s summit in Brazil and more than the combined delegations of all 14 Pacific Small Island Developing States, according to an analysis of U.N. participant lists by the Center for International Environmental Law. Forty-five of those representatives were granted entry to closed-door negotiating sessions. The center has not completed a similar analysis of lobbyists for other technologies.

By Thursday, as formal climate talks continued, drafters had entirely stripped out mention of a transition away from fossil fuels while leaving the aggressive carbon capture benchmarks intact. When a final draft was proposed Sunday — two days after negotiations were scheduled to conclude — the CCS targets had been made less specific but remained, described as a nonbinding “gigatonne scale” goal.

The agreement — and its emphasis on CCS — “really had the fossil fuel industry’s fingerprints all over it,” said Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead for the nonprofit Oil Change International, a research and advocacy group pushing for a phaseout of fossil fuels.
A coalition of nations, including the European Union, rejected the proposal outright.

For years, tensions at the annual climate talks have tended to break down to three camps: Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states — at times with tacit U.S. support — which argue for an approach that prioritizes slow changes in the energy system in service of economic stability; the wealthy, industrialized nations, which push for an energy transition but resist measures to pay for both the transition and damages caused by warming; and the low- and middle-income nations, which will sign on to fossil fuel phaseout only if other powerful economies commit to supporting the cost of their transition.

Carbon capture remains just one part of that larger debate, which included other ways to clean up energy sources. But its weight in this year’s talks reflects long-standing efforts to tie climate action to its success, as well as a failure to enact any other meaningful agreement that would slow the rate of CO2 emissions in the first place.

For more than a year, ProPublica and Drilled have investigated the history of carbon capture and storage and the decades-long effort by oil companies to validate it in the scientific community and at the U.N. Our reporting has found that industry funding contributed to influential CCS research at universities, petrostates pressed the U.N. to validate the technology without supporting evidence and climate modelers have assumed it can work at an enormous scale, despite the technology’s troubled real-world track record.

In the closing session, a delegate from Panama explained that the country could not support the language in the final COP31 text in part because “it wagers too much” on CCS “instead of calling for deep changes.”

Vanuatu, a small island nation in the Pacific that is especially vulnerable to rising sea levels, warned that the text “risks legitimizing continued fossil fuel dependence” and that carbon capture must not become “an excuse to prolong the fossil fuel era.”
But Saudi Arabia, speaking on behalf of the 22 countries in the League of Arab States, insisted CCS was an essential part of a “package of solutions” to address climate change.

“If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important,” the Saudi delegate said, “it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions, which is what this COP was meant to represent, will be taken off the table.”

articles.title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
articles.author: Max Blau
paras: Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.
A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”
“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.”
“I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.

Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by refusing to cover the costs.

ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests — known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to care.

Each dot below is a marketplace plan in Texas, sized according to the number of prior authorization requests it reported in 2025. Plans further to the right deny those requests at higher rates. Ambetter plans are shown in red.

In Texas, where Ambetter’s denial rates were above 32%, the company initially refused to pay for a medical scan for a patient with Stage 4 colon cancer because the doctor hadn’t ordered a cheaper, less precise scan first.
In Iowa, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 31%, it approved a patient’s colonoscopy but denied a request for the bowel prep that all patients must drink in advance of the procedure.
In Kansas, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 26%, it stopped covering an anti-inflammatory treatment for a patient with Crohn’s disease because it wanted the patient to try a different drug.
A ProPublica analysis of nearly 200 federal marketplace plans across the country found that Ambetter had the highest denial rates in most states where it provided data.
Ambetter plans had an average denial rate of 25% in states where the company reported data for last year. That’s substantially higher than the 16% average denial rate for all marketplace plans.

Our analysis is based on data that federal regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment.

Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is largely a black box.

U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the people.”
Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further.

“This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to address the improper use of prior authorization.”
We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial.

ProPublica is looking into the ways health insurers’ use of prior authorization impacts patients. We need your help to figure out if the process is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or medication.

Sarah London, CEO of Ambetter’s parent company, Centene, recently said in a statement on its website that it was “creating a more predictable and transparent experience” for its customers. That statement followed growing backlash against the industry and a push to limit the practice of prior authorization.

Last year Centene joined America’s largest insurers in vowing to rely on prior authorization less often. Industry representatives have said that the collective efforts of those insurers will decrease their use of prior authorization across all of their plans by 11% in 2026. (Health plans aren’t required to publish 2026 data until next year.)

ProPublica sent Centene a detailed list of questions about its use of prior authorization and the impact it has on its customers. ProPublica also provided Ambetter with signed releases from customers, including Felicia, waiving their right to privacy, so that Centene representatives could speak with ProPublica about their specific denials. Centene didn’t respond to ProPublica’s questions. In a statement, a spokesperson for the company said that Ambetter is “committed to help ensure patients receive safe, appropriate, evidence-based care, and we continue to work to simplify the prior authorization process and reduce administrative burden for members and providers.”
Reached by phone, Counihan told ProPublica that he retired this year and declined to comment due to “contractual commitments” with the company that prevent him from doing so.
Listen to Ambetter’s Then-CEO
Kevin Counihan tells a customer he can’t approve coverage of the treatment her doctor sought.

For some Ambetter customers, the consequences of prior authorization denials were particularly stark, leading to delayed tests and disrupted treatments. A small fraction of those customers got Ambetter to cover their care after complaining to powerful politicians. One Ambetter customer who was denied routine bloodwork complained to a state agency. Another who had been denied cancer treatment asked a U.S. senator for help.

Even though Felicia’s complaint made it all the way up to powerful politicians — and she had pressed Centene’s C-suite to get in touch — she was disheartened by what Counihan ultimately would have to say.

Felicia had lost track of all the hours spent on curbing her weight, going so far as to try three different anti-obesity medications. During the follow-up call, Counihan explained that didn’t actually have the authority to help with the fourth.
“Do what you need to do,” Counihan responded. “Escalate it in any way that you can.”
This spring, as Richie Jones recovered from having his tumor-filled prostate removed, he received some troubling news. The cancer was still in his body.

The 49-year-old drummer from Atlanta’s suburbs was willing to do anything to get more time with his wife and daughter. His oncologist said the best option was to shoot a pencil-sized beam of protons at the cancer that remained, zapping it out of existence. That kind of therapy can cost far more than standard radiation but inflicts far less damage to the rest of the body.

First, though, his oncologist had to confirm that Ambetter would cover proton therapy. He asked the insurer to approve it in advance, as it required. Ambetter denied the request based on a recommendation from an oncologist working with the insurer.

Insurers have varying policies on whether to cover proton therapy for patients with prostate cancer. In recent years, insurance researchers have found that patients with commercial plans who are facing a denial for proton therapy for a variety of cancers have a good shot of getting it overturned on appeal.
Jones’ oncologist appealed. That, too, was denied. Ambetter explained its decision in a letter to Jones, claiming he did “not have a type of cancer this treatment is used for.”
What angered Jones most was that there was a different doctor advising Ambetter on the denial of the appeal, and that doctor didn’t specialize in proton therapy, let alone cancer. It was an OB-GYN.

Fearful that his cancer would spread more, Jones emailed Ambetter’s support department, hoping to break through to whatever human was on the other end. “You have the power to allow my child to have her daddy around for years to come,” he wrote.

When people actually fight prior authorization denials, they have a good shot at winning. ProPublica’s analysis found that more than half of Ambetter customers who contested their denials had them overturned. But the vast majority of the time, denials go uncontested. Only 7% of prior authorization denials by Ambetter were challenged last year, the analysis found.

Marketplace plan holders told ProPublica that they didn’t appeal because they didn’t know about their rights or how to navigate the process. Insurance experts and advocates say that patience and persistence are required to fight a denial.
Ambetter Customers Have a Good Shot at Overturning Their Denials. Few of Them Try.
Most prior authorization denials are never appealed. More often than not, Ambetter customers who appeal get approved after going through a complex process.

On the other side of metro Atlanta from Jones, 48-year-old artist Travis Christopher was trying to get treatment for his liver cancer last year. After getting so sick that he left his job — and lost the insurance that came with it — he bought an Ambetter plan on the marketplace.

It covered a specialized treatment by his oncologist, who placed a wire of irradiated beads in his liver to precisely target his tumor. But to know if the radiation worked, his oncologist needed CT scans.

Ambetter denied three different requests for prior authorization for the scans. After a month of delays, Christopher complained to his state senator, saying that he was “stuck waiting until Ambetter decides whether or not I live or die.” The state senator passed it along to Georgia’s insurance commissioner. Soon after, Ambetter overturned the denial and agreed to cover the care.

Every day of delay can increase the odds that cancer spreads. No one can say how much the wait affected Christopher’s prognosis. What is certain is that Christopher’s health got worse in the months ahead. He died this past winter, shortly after his daughter was born.

Jones was able to get care in time. Like Christopher, he worked to draw attention to Ambetter’s denial. He contacted local journalists, wrote to the office of the U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, and filed a complaint with Georgia’s insurance commissioner. In late June, after getting in touch with staffers in both officials’ offices, Jones received a call from Emory Healthcare: Their oncologists were ready to start.
Ambetter had decided to reverse its denial.

Over the course of his nearly 40 rounds of proton therapy, Jones realized that he wanted others to know the importance of fighting back. So he granted permission to Ossoff to publish what had happened in a report on prior authorization denials. In a statement to ProPublica, Ossoff said that he has “heard from too many Georgians who get a cancer diagnosis, and then instead of being free to fight their cancer, they have to fight their insurance company.”
“We need to ban health insurance companies from denying or delaying needed health care,” Ossoff said in the statement.
Several months later, Jones stood in the lobby of Emory’s cancer center. Surrounded by his family and friends, he rang a ceremonial bell hanging on the wall, marking the end of his treatment.
It was only after he was in remission that Jones would begin to see just how much his complaint had mattered.

With Jones’ permission, ProPublica obtained records this month that shed light on why Ambetter changed its decision about the proton therapy. The records include a letter Ambetter sent to Georgia’s insurance commissioner’s office that explained the rationale for each of its denials. In the letter, the insurer wrote that it had decided, two days after Jones filed his complaint, to consult clinical guidelines used by America’s leading oncologists in determining how to proceed with covering his treatment. Ambetter previously had relied on a more restrictive guideline from a contractor that handles its prior authorization requests for cancer treatment.
“Why wasn’t that their guideline in the first place?” Jones said. “Why does it take being a squeaky wheel to have them change their mind?”

In June 2025, following a meeting with U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Centene and other large insurers promised to reduce the volume of medical services subject to prior authorization. Centene has since touted “measurable progress” toward fulfilling that promise. The company didn’t answer ProPublica’s questions about whether Ambetter’s prior authorization use has gone down this year.
But insurance experts, consumer advocates and lawmakers question how far those promises go.

Wendell Potter, a former Cigna executive turned consumer advocate, recently wrote that these commitments rely on “an impressive-sounding number to mislead.” For instance, he said that UnitedHealthcare promised a 30% drop in prior authorization requirements, but only 2% of covered medical services are eligible for the more relaxed requirements. (UnitedHealthcare spokesperson Eric Hausman told ProPublica that the insurer has been “transparent” about its efforts to reduce the use of prior authorization and has already enacted some of them.)

Brit Vanneman, a staff attorney for the National Health Law Program, wrote that these commitments “may simply be a strategic attempt to deflect growing public criticism” regarding prior authorization.
“The commitments are vague,” Vanneman told ProPublica. “There’s a lot of fluff.”
What isn’t vague: the continued impact of prior authorization denials since the industry’s pledge.
“I still do not have a CT scan scheduled, and am stuck waiting until Ambetter decides whether or not I live or die.”Travis Christopher, in an email to his state senator in September 2025

Two women got their denials overturned by Ambetter only after posting about them on social media. One, a Florida mother, told ProPublica she bought an Ambetter plan because her previous insurer stopped covering autism therapy for her 6-year-old son. The Ambetter plan she chose had covered other children seen by the providers who’d treated her son for the past two years. But Ambetter denied the request for his treatment this year, and her son’s care was put on pause.

The other, a Kansas woman, said Ambetter denied a drug infusion to treat her Crohn’s disease last year. She said this was shocking to her, since for the previous two years Ambetter had covered the infusion, which worked better for her than anything else she tried.
Both women’s social media posts prompted Ambetter reps to reach out to them directly, saying they wanted to address their problems. And indeed, the ordered treatments were provided.

Felicia wasn’t as fortunate. After Ambetter’s CEO expressed sympathy and encouraged her to fight for her obesity treatment, she moved forward with the final step in the process: asking an independent company to review her appeal.

At that point, Felicia had spent two years on three different weight-loss drugs that were covered by Ambetter, including the popular GLP-1 drug Ozempic. But those drugs had caused side effects, such as insomnia and migraines. When she was prescribed samples of tirzepatide, another GLP-1, by her doctor in 2023, everything finally clicked: She lost a significant amount of weight over two months without any side effects.
But Ambetter was not willing to cover Zepbound, the tirzepatide her doctor prescribed.
As a way to keep costs down, health insurers tend to deny requests for GLP-1s not listed on their formularies. When that happens, a customer can appeal and seek a formulary exception.

In September 2024, she asked her endocrinologist to support her appeal. He explained in a letter that a denial of this particular GLP-1 “could significantly hinder her progress and potentially lead to worsening of her condition, which could result in more intensive and costly interventions in the future.” As he saw it, this GLP-1 was “the most appropriate and potentially life-saving medication,” especially given Felicia’s other overlapping medical conditions.

But that November, the company overseeing the independent review declined to consider her appeal, writing that an appeal involving a medication that wasn’t on a health plan’s approved drug list was “outside of our scope of review.” In other words, Felicia had hit a dead end.

Felicia has continued struggling with obesity ever since the Zepbound denial. She’s also experienced worsening symptoms for several other chronic conditions, including persistent migraines. Felicia said she has nine each month on average, and medical experts say that obesity is a strong risk factor for migraines. But Ambetter has denied prior authorization for numerous migraine medications prescribed by her doctors.

Ambetter is the only insurance Felicia had ever bought. By this fall, she had become so fed up with the denials that she contacted an insurance broker to help her find another marketplace plan during open enrollment. But the quotes she received for various plans were either much higher than Ambetter’s or didn’t provide access to her doctors. If she wanted to clear the hurdles she’d faced, the cost would be far more than she could possibly afford.
It left her with a sinking feeling: Ambetter might be her only viable option.
The post Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients. appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
articles.author: Alec MacGillis
paras: Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the planned departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.
Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.
Do You Have a Tip for ProPublica?
If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s decision to retire as head of the Smithsonian at the end of the year, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

As recounted by ProPublica in September, the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.

By the time of Trump’s return to office in 2025, there was no shortage of fodder for the new administration to seize on. The July report noted a recent exhibit on Ben Franklin that speculated about whether he had used enslaved members of his household as subjects of his experiments with electric shocks. And it chastised the museum for having trained staff using the “Museums as a Site for Social Action Toolkit,” a 200-plus-page tract on how to “truly transform the museum space,” which it says is linked “with white supremacy, hetero-patriarchy, abuse of labor, colonization, imperialist theft of art and artifacts, destruction or absencing of alternative ways of interpreting or representing art and artifacts, structural racism and other oppressions.”

The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated, “including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the development that led our nation to where it is today.”

The report was released with symbolic fanfare on the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding. The administration’s announcement of its next move on this front may have less pop, given its soft rollout on the Orange Line.
