articles.title: If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported?
paras: About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk.

I’m a ProPublica reporter in Detroit, and my colleague Melissa Sanchez is in Chicago. We each drove over 100 miles last summer to be in this room because we were working on a story. It published in mid-October, and it’s about how the immigration policies of President Donald Trump’s administration have made life more perilous for victims of domestic abuse. While reporting, we had heard about the pervasive presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in west Michigan, and we wanted to hear from immigrant women there who were living through domestic abuse. How did they weigh whether it was safer to stay with an abusive partner or to seek help from law enforcement, knowing they might be detained — and even deported?

That night, a young woman with a toddler told us that she called 911 about a year earlier, after her boyfriend slapped her when he was drunk. If he hit her today, she said, she wouldn’t dial that number again. With arrests by federal immigration officers constantly in the news, she said, the risk is too great.

None of the others in the room said they were currently living with an abusive partner. Those women were out there, the group’s facilitators told us. But they were too afraid to even leave their homes.

After the meeting, as empty paper plates were cleared from the tables, the facilitators told us about E. She was once a regular at the meetings, they said, but hadn’t been around in a while. They worried about her. We asked if E. might be open to talking with us and, after a few texts, we learned that she was — if we could be ready to talk in about 20 minutes.

We hurried back to our nearby lodgings, dialed E.’s number and put her on speakerphone. In Spanish, Melissa explained what we were reporting on, why it was so important to hear from somebody like her and the kinds of questions we wanted to ask. Then we began the interview.

E., who asked not to be fully identified, told us that she avoids going out unless it’s absolutely necessary. She’d heard harrowing stories about women at the immigration detention center in Michigan where other women we’d interviewed were locked up. As we described in our story, several had been arrested here in Kent County when local police responded to domestic violence calls. E. doesn’t want to end up in ICE custody herself or, worse, deported.
For the sake of her kids, E. said, she tolerates her husband’s abuse in silence.

When he tells her she’s “nobody here” and to “go back to your country,” she said she puts her head down. When he pulls her hair in bed and says she belongs to him, she said she pretends it’s a joke. When he asks for the money she makes from selling food at a local factory, she said she hands it over.

A filing in E.’s immigration case says her husband is a U.S. citizen who has been “verbally and financially abusive” and has threatened to take away the child they share. E. said that, except for the hair pulling, he isn’t physically abusive.
For help in English or Spanish, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text “start” to 88788.

(Like the other women we interviewed, E. asked that ProPublica not interview her alleged abuser because she’s afraid he will retaliate against her, take away her children or call ICE. To report these women’s stories, we interviewed attorneys, advocates, family and others who interacted with them. When available, we also reviewed text messages, and records from law enforcement and immigration court.)

E. said her husband doesn’t overtly threaten her with calling ICE. But she said she found a hotline number for the agency written in his journal, alongside a description of his ideal woman: obedient and submissive.

That reminded us of what a local immigration attorney, Catherine Villanueva, had told us: “We have this idea that we’re deporting these really bad people,” she said. “What we’re doing is we’re empowering the bad people who are already here.”

We asked E. if she had ever called the police to report her husband’s abuse. Her answer came quickly: No. Her husband is frail. She worries police officers will look at both of them and decide that he’s the victim. “They won’t see me as the abused one,” she said. “If I called the police, the one who would wind up losing is me.”

When we reached out to federal officials for our story, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” As part of our reporting, we examined the backgrounds of the women we interviewed. Most had no criminal records we could find.

People in law enforcement and the prosecutor’s office in Kent County told us that they wanted everybody to feel safe reaching out to report crimes, regardless of their immigration status. Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker said that he and a Spanish-speaking assistant prosecutor met with local advocates for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence “to try and lower that barrier, to make people understand that we see them as victims and want to serve them as victims.”
“But,” he added, “we can talk all we want, and still, I think it’s still difficult.”

Indeed, Angelica Ferrer, the victim witness coordinator in Becker’s office, said she used to be able to tell victims that if they came to court, “we’re not going to have ICE here.” She doesn’t say that to them anymore. “That is a choice that you have to make,” she said. “I can’t guarantee that you won’t be stopped on the way to court.”

Providing support for immigrants who are domestic abuse victims has long been extraordinarily difficult. But over five months of reporting, Melissa and I kept coming up against the same pervasive fear: In the current climate, nobody can really keep them safe.

Yet we heard from a lot of folks in Kent County who are trying to reach people like E., whether from positions in law enforcement, via social service agencies or as volunteers. Mary Sue Stegehuis, a retired teacher, is involved with a grassroots group called Hope for Neighbors. Even though she doesn’t know Spanish, she visits women in ICE custody, usually with a bilingual friend, and she stays in touch with them through a messaging app. She prints their stories — many involving domestic abuse — on homemade prayer cards, with an image of Mary, Joseph and Jesus migrating from Egypt on one side. Sharing the cards with others in the community, she told us, is meant to ensure that their stories don’t disappear, even if the women aren’t in the room to tell them.

We are still reporting on immigration and domestic abuse. If you have a tip or expertise, or you just want to share something you know, please get in touch. I’m at 313-310-6592, on both cell and Signal, and anna.clark@propublica.org, and Melissa is at 872-444-0011, on both cell and Signal, and melissa.sanchez@propublica.org.

articles.title: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
articles.author: Katie Worth
paras: You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.

Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise, particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage. CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea.
At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.

Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey, for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of decades.

Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year, the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits annually.
Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains unproven?
Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already presumed that it will work.

I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re wrong, Miami could pay the price.

One chart laid bare to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely spot a panel out the nearest window:
Carbon Capture Capacity Has Never Come Close to Projections
Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing projections.

I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity. But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every assumption they build into their influential simulations.
So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:
Climate models assume it’s easy and efficient to capture carbon. It’s not.

Public data is hard to come by, but several analyses have found the real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates would increase.
They don’t account for problems that come up in real-world practice.

In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people in the industry.
They assume the Earth is a bottomless geologic landfill.

Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, a paper in the journal Nature warned that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine, the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite, the real potential may be “smaller.”
They assume that stored CO2 will stay put.

Scientists warn that even tiny annual leak rates over longtime horizons could undermine a storage site’s climate benefit. Our investigation found two large-scale sites that have leaked, one all the way to the surface. Surely the models all factor in this risk? I asked Detlef van Vuuren, leader of the Dutch model, if his did so. His one-word answer: “Nope.”
The models all assume CCS gets more affordable over time, though real-world costs have steadily climbed.

When I asked Strefler if it makes sense to assume our children and grandchildren will pay big bucks to suck CO2 out of the air, even though today governments won’t spend pennies to avoid emitting that pollution, she said: “If a country is not willing to do that, I don’t see how they would be willing to” pay for CO2 removal.

In short, the modelers overlooked decades of underperformance, inflated capture rates, evidence of leaks and finite underground storage, all while assuming future generations will willingly bankroll an increasingly expensive industry. They pointed to a mix of legitimate studies to support those assertions. They also pointed to unreviewed white papers, casual chats with industry insiders and the 2005 U.N. report — of which van Vuuren was an author. Van Vuuren said his team is working to revise some of its assumptions, but he generally sees no technical reason why CCS cannot work, or should be excluded from the possibilities his model considers. He said it is a policy decision whether countries wish to invest the dollars and effort to make it happen.

One way to look at the model projections is as recipes for the future. Seen this way, the modelers’ argument is that their job is to assemble a cookbook, not tell us how each recipe tastes. In other words, the models merely show that if CCS works and is used at an extraordinary scale, it is possible to hit climate targets. And the modelers told ProPublica and Drilled that the delay in climate action has left few other tools to do so — and so they include CCS.

A good recipe, though, cannot rely on imaginary ingredients. If we’re making unrealistic assumptions, why not include the possibility that aliens will appear and hand us a solution to climate change, I asked Riahi, half joking.
“You can quote me that I think carbon dioxide removal is more likely than an alien,” Riahi said.
Note on Data Sources for the Charts

The 2008 and 2010 projections are from the IEA’s Blue Map scenario; a second 2010 projection is from the Net Zero by 2050 scenario; 2018 is from the Sustainable Development scenario; and 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 are from the Announced Pledges, Stated Policies and Net Zero by 2050 scenarios. Some of these scenarios represent pathways designed to achieve a specific temperature or concentration of CO2. Other scenarios represent what is possible based on current policies or pledges. Pathways from years where underlying data was not provided in the IEA’s report were excluded.
The post Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology? appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
articles.author: Josh Hinkle
paras: Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing.
His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement.

“I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000.
It stands to earn much more.

Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year.

Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key incentive for local governments across the country has long been the funding that comes with participation.

The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments.

The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time spent,” he said.

And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature” could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and money for overtime.
“How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner John Moore asked.
“Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.

Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it difficult to pull away from the program in the future.
“I’m concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of these small police departments,” she said.
In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations, in addition to immigration work.

The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and “fleet purchases.”
Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our everyday job,” Fowler said.

Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets dangerous criminal offenders.

Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN’s questions about the department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by phone, email and in person.
“We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie Galloway, the only official to respond.

Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money is spent.

KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300 people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60 days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if an agreement is terminated.

That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.
Between the end of April and mid-June, it made two.
Local law enforcement agencies that join forces with ICE can choose among three models, two of which focus on identifying people already in jail who may be subject to deportation.

Trump revived the third kind, called the task force model, at the beginning of his second term. Task force agreements often worry civil and immigrants’ rights groups because of the model’s problematic track record: ICE started phasing them out in 2012, after Department of Justice investigations revealed that sheriff’s offices participating in the model had committed civil rights violations.
But task force agreements can also be lucrative.

Agencies can receive federal reimbursement for salaries, overtime and benefits for “conducting purposeful and intentional” immigration enforcement activities once the contract starts, according to a service agreement obtained by KXAN.

They can also get recurring quarterly incentive payments and one-time stipends for equipment, technology and vehicles, though federal memoranda and agreements obtained by KXAN don’t specify what agencies can purchase.

The Department of Homeland Security stopped renewing task force model agreements during the Obama administration after federal investigations revealed civil rights violations involving sheriffs’ offices in Arizona and North Carolina.

Since Trump’s return to office, the model has become the most common of the three agreement types. At least 241 task force model agreements were signed in Texas in 2026 alone, compared to just 30 combined for the other models in that time period, according to ICE participation data from September.
Smith County was among the first in Texas to sign on after the president reinstated the task force model in early 2025.
Moore, the only member of Smith County’s Commissioners Court who agreed to speak with KXAN, explained why he thought the commissioners wanted to partner.
His first word: “budgetary.”

“Any kind of training that any of our departments need to have, or are required to have, costs money, and it’s rare that we get an opportunity to get funding for training from outside county taxes,” Moore said. “Any time we can save the taxpayers money, I’m all for it.”

Smith County got more money than any other of the 93 Texas law enforcement agencies whose funding KXAN reviewed. The sheriff’s office received nearly $2.2 million in federal 287(g) funding from January 2025 to June 2026, according to records obtained by KXAN. That’s equivalent to about 12% of its budget for fiscal year 2025.

Smith, the sheriff, told the Commissioners Court last November that although vehicles purchased with that money would be used for the 287(g) program, “that doesn’t mean, if we’re out here, we won’t run to another call or take another call that comes across the radio. We will do that. We try not to separate 287(g) from our other law enforcement duties. We do it all together.”

About 120 of 198 licensed officers in the Smith County Sheriff’s Office participated in the program. Together, they conducted 124 immigration enforcement actions between October 2025 and July. KXAN requested a list of 287(g) stops from the department, in addition to any associated charge. Smith County listed no associated criminal charge for more than 100 of these stops.
Jose Rodriguez and his 23-year-old son, Pablo Rodriguez, were among those affected.

One afternoon in late June, the pair cruised along Loop 323, a circular segment of highway in Tyler, a city of 113,000 people in East Texas. They’d spent hours working in the summer heat at a construction job and were headed to Chick-fil-A to pick up lunch for their family.

Then red and blue lights appeared behind them. The law enforcement agent said that he’d pulled their black extended-cab work truck over because of a missing license plate on the trailer attached to the pickup and a missing dual-wheel mud flap.

Body and vehicle camera footage showed the detective requesting that Jose Rodriguez get out of the truck. “Any English at all?” the detective later asked. Jose Rodriguez raised his right hand, holding his thumb and index finger close together.
“Un poquito?” the detective asked, followed by, “Are you a U.S. citizen?”
The man shook his head and answered. “No.”
Seconds later, the detective pulled Jose Rodriguez’s hands behind his back and put him in handcuffs.

He was eventually taken from the Smith County jail to an ICE detention facility, about two hours west of Tyler. His son, who is a U.S. citizen, said Jose Rodriguez was detained for about three months before being deported to Mexico.
KXAN could find no criminal convictions or arrests on his record when the Smith County detective took him into custody in June.
“Just like that, he’s gone,” Pablo Rodriguez later told KXAN. “My dad’s gone.”

Law enforcement officers, Pablo Rodriguez said, “portray us as criminals, rapists, violent people. We’re not that. We’re just regular people trying to find a better life. The only difference is our skin. That’s pretty much it.”
The Future of the Program in Texas
Elections earlier this month have left the 287(g) program’s future uncertain, at least in Texas.

While the Trump administration has reached agreements with local law enforcement to work with immigration officials, Congress has broader oversight authority. That includes decisions about funding. In January, Democrats will take over both chambers of Congress and many, including freshman Texas Sen. James Talarico, have criticized ICE tactics. It’s unclear, however, how much of their focus will be on immigration enforcement and specifically on the 287(g) program.

More locally, state Sen. Charles Schwertner, the Republican lawmaker who authored a measure in 2025 that required most Texas sheriff’s offices to participate in the program, wants to expand the mandate during the coming legislative session to include other law enforcement agencies, like police departments. So does the conservative think tank where Blair works.
But support for such legislation may be harder to get after November’s midterm election.

Schwertner retained his state Senate seat, and Republicans maintained their majority in that chamber, but Democrats took control of the governor’s mansion and the state House of Representatives for the first time in a generation. Any new bills would require legislative approval from both chambers and the governor’s signature, or enough legislative support to override a veto.

In a press release well before the election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa called on Gov. Greg Abbott to “demand accountability from the Trump administration and stop enabling ICE operations that are terrorizing communities and violating the law.” The release did not mention the 287(g) program by name. Hinojosa beat Abbott in this month’s election and will take over as governor in January. She did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

The state program could also be affected by this month’s election of Democrats Nathan Johnson, who won the race for state attorney general, and Sarah Eckhardt, who won her bid to become state comptroller.

Johnson, as a state senator, opposed the mandate that sheriffs’ offices participate in the program. He will inherit responsibility for enforcing the law, which requires most sheriffs to seek agreements with ICE by Dec. 1. Johnson said he will use his discretion in deciding whether to sue sheriffs who fail to comply if they have “legitimate law enforcement reasons for not having a 287(g) agreement.”
He also questioned the state attorney general’s continued participation in the program. Current Attorney General Ken Paxton signed a 287(g) task force model agreement in February 2025.

“The attorney general’s office has tremendous, vast responsibilities,” Johnson said. “Never included among them since the creation of this state was outsourcing your employees to a federal agency for a purpose in which we’re not trained or qualified and which distracts me from the mission of my office.”
Johnson didn’t entirely rule out working with ICE in some capacity if it allowed his office to investigate crimes committed by ICE agents in Texas.

Eckhardt, meanwhile, will take over oversight of a $20 million grant program that state lawmakers created two years ago to help sheriff’s offices cover any costs of participation in the 287(g) program not reimbursed by the federal government. By late September, the comptroller’s office had awarded more than $6.5 million to 78 sheriff’s offices, according to figures obtained by KXAN.

During her campaign, Eckhardt warned that expenses for the program could eventually fall on local taxpayers, calling it “unsustainable.” After winning her seat, she said she would “do a 287(g) audit to show how that expense is driving up property taxes.”
This story is an adaptation of an investigation by KXAN. Read the original reporting:
Even if state leaders don’t expand the participation requirement or remove the current mandate, departments can choose to keep collecting federal money to enforce immigration law.

In Fayette County southeast of Austin, Sheriff’s Lt. David Beyer told KXAN that the 287(g) funding his office had already received totaled about $800,000, which helps purchase equipment it can also use for ordinary police work.
“If they want to pay us extra to do that job,” Beyer said, “we’re more than happily going to accept those funds, because that saves our taxpayers money.”
The post A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More. appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
articles.author: Anna Clark
paras: When a biotech company named AquaBounty Technologies announced plans to farm genetically engineered Atlantic salmon at a new plant in Ohio, local and state officials eagerly provided it with incentives. Not long after, the company paused construction and auctioned off “new” and “unused” equipment. Now, the state’s private economic development arm wants its $1 million back.

JobsOhio has requested repayment from AquaBounty by Sunday, according to a company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing also notes that, at the end of September, AquaBounty was down to three employees and $122,255 in cash.

AquaBounty said that its salmon could thrive in indoor freshwater farms and help feed the world. Announced in 2021, the new development in Pioneer, Ohio, was supposed to be its first large-scale production facility.
The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. It was believed to be the largest investment ever in rural Williams County.
But AquaBounty, which had never made a profit over its 30 years in business, faced a tangle of regulatory challenges and pushback from environmentalists.

Locals were also suspicious of how the village mayor’s personal interests were tied up in the project. Among other moves, Pioneer Mayor Ed Kidston bought land that AquaBounty wanted to build on. He then sold it to the company for $1.5 million more than he’d paid.

AquaBounty’s plan was unproven, but, as ProPublica reported last year, the company was buoyed by state and local resources — including the million-dollar grant from JobsOhio. The company received the money in August 2021, according to financial filings, shortly after the project went public.

“Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling,” said Sherry Fleming of Williams County Alliance, a grassroots environmental group. While AquaBounty had genetic engineering know-how, she said it seemed to have limited experience in production.

In response to ProPublica’s queries, a press contact for AquaBounty said it shares what it can in its SEC releases and filings, and that it’s still in discussion with JobsOhio over the repayment demand. AquaBounty’s filing said that “there can be no assurance that JobsOhio will agree to any payment schedule or other accommodation.”
“Any collection or legal action by JobsOhio could result in additional costs and management distraction,” it added.

Kidston didn’t respond to requests for comment. He said at the time that his actions involving the plant were intended only to help the community. The village administrator referred ProPublica to AquaBounty and its website.

JobsOhio operates privately but has a funding mechanism set up by the state and a board appointed by the governor. Matt Englehart, a spokesperson for JobsOhio, said in an email to ProPublica that it “operates with transparency and accountability,” but its limited disclosures have long been a sore point for Ohioans.

On its website, JobsOhio says its funding model for specialized grants is “independent” and accommodating of “unique needs.” Qualifications include, but aren’t limited to, “job creation, additional payroll, fixed-asset investment commitment, project return on investment, and project location.”

The AquaBounty grant depended on not only the creation of jobs, but also $222 million in capital investment and a payroll of more than $5.4 million by the end of 2026. It had to maintain those commitments through the end of 2028.
Less than two years after it got the money, construction stalled. Roughly 30% built, the site languished at the end of Kexon Drive, a smooth new road that Pioneer had extended for its benefit.

AquaBounty sold equipment intended for the Ohio farm in 2024 and 2025. It also sold its intellectual property for genetically engineered salmon. By the end of September, according to its filing, its primary remaining assets were unsold equipment, the land in Pioneer and the incomplete build.

JobsOhio and other economic development boosters should “take a good look at this because they’re putting taxpayer dollars at risk when they advertise to bring these industries in, and they haven’t done their homework to protect the community,” Fleming said. (JobsOhio is funded by profits from state-controlled liquor sales, not by taxes.)

Englehart told ProPublica that he can’t discuss a situation that may result in litigation. But with any company, he said, “when metric commitments are not met, we work closely with those businesses” to help them overcome challenges.
If all options are exhausted, he added, “we will claw back some or all of our dollars so they can be used for future economic development projects to benefit Ohioans.”

JobsOhio’s demand notice came in September, the financial filing said, informing the company that its equipment sales and consideration of acquisition offers for the Ohio farm were a breach of the grant agreement.

AquaBounty “provided additional information” to JobsOhio in October, the filing said, but the agency upheld its demand and requested repayment this month. If it doesn’t come, the filing said, JobsOhio may refer the matter for collections and “pursue the remedies available” under the grant agreement.

With an onerous process and uncertain outcomes, it’s “pretty rare” for JobsOhio to try to claw back money, said Kristan Wong Karinen, a research analyst with the nonprofit Good Jobs First, which tracks public subsidies in economic development. More commonly, she said, it and other agencies will renegotiate the contract — extending the time period for a company to meet commitments, perhaps, or lowering requirements.
“In this case, with AquaBounty,” Wong Karinen said, “because they haven’t done anything, they haven’t fulfilled any of the requirements, I feel like JobsOhio is being forced into this.”

articles.title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
articles.author: Cassandra Garibay
paras: When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt.

The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California.
“I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?”

If you receive SNAP benefits, Joly’s experience may sound all too familiar. Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households.

ProPublica recently published an investigation into why Congress and the Trump administration have failed to crack down on SNAP theft despite promises to tackle fraud and waste in safety-net programs. As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted.

Many of the victims we heard from had similar questions: How did this happen? How can I prevent it from happening again? Why am I not being reimbursed? And why does it seem like little is being done to prevent these crimes in the first place?

We spoke with dozens of federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, caseworkers, food security advocates and other experts to help answer these questions for you.
How does SNAP theft happen?

Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install “skimming” devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When you swipe your card, these devices capture your data off the magnetic strip on the back, as well as your PIN. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby.

Skimming is largely preventable via microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have been greatly successful in reducing fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.

In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with these scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case, a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits.
What can I do to protect my benefits?

Unfortunately, due to the government’s inaction, the burden of protecting benefits from being stolen has largely been left up to you, the individual SNAP recipient. And the options are less than ideal.

Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel, allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use. These apps may also allow you to change your PIN and block out-of-state or online transactions.
But these aren’t always practical solutions, many victims told us. Remembering new PINs all the time, for example, isn’t easy, especially for older beneficiaries.

Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she wasn’t using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits.
“I was simply unable to do whatever the steps were, no matter how hard I tried,” she said.

Besides card locking and changing PINs, the Secret Service has suggested that people may be able to spot evidence of tampering with card readers at grocery stores. For example, if you look closely at the reader and see a noticeable gap between the keypad and the rest of the device, or if you see that something is blocking the light from under the keys, there may be a skimming device there.
What can I do after my benefits have been stolen?

If you’ve had your SNAP benefits stolen, you can report the theft to your state or local social services office — the agency where you applied for SNAP — or to the EBT card customer service line on the back of your card to receive a new card and change your PIN so thieves can’t continue to access your benefits.

You can also report the crime to local law enforcement and to the agency within your state in charge of investigating SNAP fraud — for example, in Texas, SNAP theft victims are advised to report it to the Texas Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. (This map shows where to report SNAP fraud for each state).

A representative for Texas Health and Human Services said, “HHSC takes the security of our client’s benefits very seriously. SNAP card skimming has been a persistent problem across the country, including Texas.”

While there have been some large-scale investigations into SNAP theft, individual reports don’t often lead to an arrest. More than 40 of the victims we heard from said that they had reported their stolen benefits to a SNAP office, the EBT card customer service line, the police or all of the above. A handful also called the stores where they’d noticed unrecognized transactions on their card history, and two said they contacted the FBI. Most were told nothing could be done.

“I was told that I will receive another card in the mail and that I will not get the money back,” one person wrote us. “They took my statement but said they couldn’t help,” wrote another. “No one ever followed up,” said a third.

The main benefit of reporting these thefts is that doing so keeps the issue on the radar of SNAP officials. Many program administrators and caseworkers told us that they feel the urgency of this crisis precisely because so many people have been calling in about it.
Will my stolen benefits be replaced?

In all but two states (California and Maryland), your benefits will not be reimbursed.The federal government had been reinstating stolen SNAP funds in all 50 states starting in late 2022. However, at the end of 2024, an effort to extend that reimbursement system was quashed after Elon Musk posted more than a hundred social media messages opposing legislation that included it, as the Department of Government Efficiency era began. (Musk did not reply to a previous request for comment.)
Democrats in Congress have proposed legislation to restart the reimbursement program. Following the recent midterm elections, they will take power in January.
How does law enforcement investigate SNAP theft?

As ProPublica has reported, the Secret Service devotes a lot of investigative resources to this issue, with teams going store to store around the country to manually check card readers for skimming devices. But that’s not a very efficient approach — it’s a little like playing whack-a-mole, multiple Secret Service agents told us.

Local cops and state prosecutors, meanwhile, are often overmatched, having neither the jurisdiction nor the technical chops to catch scammers who are constantly crossing county, state and international lines. And the feds, who do have the capacity to bring interstate conspiracy charges, haven’t always shown an interest in doing so, given that these are considered relatively low-level cases compared with the other types of crime that federal prosecutors work on.
As for caseworkers, most can’t offer concrete help. Several said that all they can do is provide a list of local food banks.
Will chip cards help prevent theft?
If your benefits were stolen, there’s a good chance they were skimmed. And the best solution to skimming appears to be tap-to-pay EBT cards with microchips.
In California, where chip cards were implemented independent of federal efforts, reported theft of SNAP and other benefits decreased by more than 80% within two years.

Following ProPublica’s reporting in October, the federal Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP, announced plans to require all 50 states to adopt more secure card technology. But overhauling the SNAP payment system could take years, as well as additional funding from Congress.

The chip card transition comes at a time when social benefits are being drastically cut and more of the financial weight of SNAP is being shifted to the states. Issuing these new cards is likely to cost states millions, involving complicated negotiations with EBT card companies like FIS and Conduent, which are essentially the Visa and Mastercard of SNAP. Grocery stores, bodegas and any places that accept EBT will also need to update their card reader systems. It will be mostly up to states to notify local stores about this and help them with it, which some, like California, Alabama and Oklahoma, have already tried to do.
Do You Administer SNAP or Medicaid Benefits? Help ProPublica Report on America’s Safety Net.

While ProPublica is no longer gathering information about people’s experiences with SNAP theft, we are still interested in learning more about America’s changing safety net. If you work to administer SNAP or Medicaid, we want to know how the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill is shaping your work and what you are seeing and hearing from the communities you serve.
